content.logline:
Sold to settle her dead mother's debts, a sharp-tongued woman arrives at the estate of the cold-blooded financier who bought her, braced to earn her freedom — never guessing he once loved her mother, that he's been quietly handing her that freedom since the first morning, and that the last person on earth still convinced she's owned is herself.
---
we'll get a glimpse of the two main characters' lives, making them relatable. the girl lovable, the master respectable. she's intelligent and strong, full of paradoxes. he's fun, bold, greedy yet kind and loving.

shape.setup:
Mara arrives at Cassian’s estate in the rain, a ledger chained to her wrist like a mockery of a wedding band. Cassian inspects her with the bored rigor of a man appraising livestock—but when she strips naked in front of his fireplace, her defiance cuts through his performative coldness. “Check my teeth?” she asks, smirking. He blinks. The hole opens slowly: in the drawing room, he mocks her mother’s singing, calls it a “beggar’s tune.” She retaliates by daubing honey on his collarbone during a pantry spat, watching him stiffen as she licks her own finger clean. They’re both playing roles, but the stakes solidify at the market. A rival sneers, “His little slave,” and Mara seizes the moment: “He sold me to you yet?” she growls, yanking Cassian’s collar until he plays along: “Pay my debt, mistress, and I’m yours.” The rival scurries off. Cassian’s eyes blaze—pride, she’ll learn, not anger.

The fall plunges at dinner. The same rival dines at the long table; Mara catches Cassian’s lingering gaze on her, the slip that gives her away. He retaliates with calculated cruelty: “Take the plates, Mara—your hands are dirty. No one wants to see that.” She obeys, flawless in mask and posture. After the guest leaves, she finds him in the dark, furious. “You did it *too well*,” she spits. “You liked it.” He freezes. The lie of the contract—ownership as armor—cracks, but neither admits it.

The climb begins with Wenna’s onions. As she chops, the housekeeper drops the truth: she burned the letter from Mara’s mother—the one asking for shelter, affection, *anything*. “Sixpence the lot,” she murmurs. “The man’s legend can’t afford a weakness he never met.” Mara’s mother *chose silence* out of deference to Cassian’s fear. It’s not betrayal; it’s sacrifice. The revelation reframes debt as farce—everyone’s been paying for a lie. Mara’s retaliation is a comic coup: she *invites* the rival to a public auction for her contract, only to outbid him with a punchline: “I’ll buy myself, and twice over—then sell you my dirt cheap.” Cassian’s forced bid (“I don’t have the coin”) is a lie they all see through, but the rival storms off, his reputation scorched.

The storm’s consummation is the pivot. Rain traps them alone; clothes cling. She presses into him, teeth at his throat. “Still owe me something?” he growls, angry at his own surrender. She rides him on the floor, sweat gleaming. “No,” she whispers as he burns the contract. “Everything just gave me everything.” The rival’s theft of the lease follows—rumors spread, lands lost. Cassian shrugs: “Worth it.” The ending lands on shared sacrifice as comedy, not tragedy. In the kitchen, she licks honey off her finger again, eyes locked on his. “Still your mistress?” He licks his thumb, drags it across her collarbone. “Always.” The lease is ashes; the future is theirs.

content.throughline: Dramatic irony as the warmth engine: the reader is let in on the joke — she's already free, he's already in love — before either character will admit it, and the comedy is the two of them being the last to know. Every turn forces a performance and then charges for it. SETUP: both perform (he appraises, she defies); the reader gets the secret first; plant the honey motif as 'the mask slipping.' FALL (dinner): the rival's presence forces Cassian to perform cruelty — he does it too well, and the cost of the lie lands for the first time. CLIMB (Wenna's confession): the burned letter reframes the whole debt as a bill nobody actually owed — the mother chose silence to protect the legend; the currency was always fake. STORM (the contract burns): Cassian stops performing first, under cover of the storm. RESOLUTION ('Always'): she was never owned, he was never armored; pay off the honey motif — the pun closes.
content.dramaticQuestion: Who stops performing first? Will Mara quit rehearsing freedom long enough to notice the rehearsal ended before it started, and will Cassian quit performing coldness long enough to be known? The ledger is the false currency they both keep paying so they never have to pay the real one — being seen.

content.ending: She places the ashes of the contract in his palm, then kisses him with the freedom of an equal. He loses the lease on his best hunting grounds to a rival who spreads rumors about them --  a price gladly paid, gains Mara's unbreakable trust.
content.controlling_idea: When the debts of the past come due, the only currency that matters is the future you choose to build together.

content.name: The Self-Redemption
content.stake: Mara's freedom and the lawful safety of her own body — whether she walks out self-held or becomes the rival's seizable property.

couples.note: Once Mara is self-held she is beyond any creditor's reach, so Cassian's love can no longer be weaponized into a lethal claim — winning here is precisely what makes losing the legend survivable ('Worth it').

win_requires.what: Redemption extinguishes a bond and makes the contract self-held, putting the person beyond any other creditor's reach
A bonded party may match the standing price in their own name at any open sale, funded lawfully
Mara's peculium fund has reached at least the standing redemption price for her contract — capital she accumulated and kept in her own name
Her contract is brought to OPEN PUBLIC SALE — the auction she herself engineers and baits the rival into attending
Cassian withholds his own signed release and lets the freedom come from her hand — his 'I don't have the coin' a lie that leaves the winning act to Mara, not to him

content.win_condition: At an open public sale of her own contract, Mara matches the standing price in her own name with her own peculium, extinguishing the bond by FULL REDEMPTION — the contract becomes self-held and she is legally free, beyond every creditor's reach.
content.lose_condition: She fails to match the standing price and is outbid; the rival lord's coin claims her contract and she is transferred into his bondage — still property, now held by the one man whose currency is hurting Cassian through her.

content.name: The Burned Letter
content.payoff: Wenna confesses she burned the letter herself, 'sixpence the lot' — Mara's mother chose silence out of deference to Cassian's fear, not absence of love. The betrayal reframes as sacrifice, and the debt that defines Mara is exposed as a lie everyone has been paying to protect.
content.promise: Mara's mother once wrote to this house asking for shelter and was answered with silence — a wound Mara carries as proof her mother abandoned her unguarded, and that Cassian's coldness is the genuine article.

content.lie: That freedom is a destination she hasn't reached yet — a state she'll unlock once the ledger is settled and the past is answered. Everything she does inside this house — talking back, setting terms, running the power dynamic — is practice for the person she'll be afterward. A rehearsal, not the real thing. The joke the book runs against her, silently, is that there is no audience for this performance except herself: Cassian can see she's been free from the first morning, Wenna can see it, the reader can see it. She is the last to know the rehearsal ended before it started.
content.tag: Tucks a loose strand of hair behind her ear with her middle finger — a small insolence dressed up as tidiness.
content.name: Mara
content.want: To earn her freedom and dig out the truth her mother buried — and, in the meantime, to take every scrap of power no one has handed her: to talk back, set her own terms, and act free inside a house that owns her, as if daring it to correct her.
content.wound: Her mother's debts came due and the man who fathered her cleared the ledger the cheapest way the law allowed — he sold her into bondage and walked, settling a debt she never signed with the only collateral he had left: her own daughter. And the mother who loved her most sang at her work and never once warned her the day was coming, so the deepest love she ever knew was also the love that left her unguarded when the bill arrived.
content.idiolect: Mock-sweet, weaponized courtesy. Answers questions with sharper questions; awards ironic honorifics to people she's deflecting ('optimists,' 'tax collectors'). Declaratives filed to a point. Never asks for a thing outright — makes the room offer it.

content.name: The Legend
content.stake: Whether being known is fatal — whether Cassian can stop performing coldness and openly love Mara without it being the thing that kills her.

win_requires.what: Public reputation is fragile currency, and visible softness in a powerful man paints a target on whoever he loves
Household knowledge converts to leverage — the rival's retaliation travels as rumor, the same channel as Wenna's burned letter
Mara is self-held and beyond every creditor's reach BEFORE the exposure lands — the redemption already won, so the target has nothing to bite
Cassian has accepted the material cost of being known — that the dinner's read, the rumors, and the best hunting lease are the price, and chosen to pay it

content.win_condition: Cassian's love for Mara becomes fully public — the cold legend spent, the lease lost to the rival's rumors, the contract burned to ashes in her palm — and it paints no lethal target on her, because she is already self-held and unseizable when he lets himself be known.
content.lose_condition: His softness is exposed while Mara is still bonded and seizable: the rival reads the man with a heart, and the rumor marks her for ruin exactly as it once destroyed her mother — the love becomes the wound.

content.lie: That a man like him can only keep safe what he keeps owned — that the contract is armor, not a leash. To let Mara go free and be openly his would only paint the same target on her that ruined her mother, so the one thing he can't afford to give her is the love that would expose her.
content.tag: Turns a heavy signet ring on his finger — once, twice — right before he lies about why he did something kind.
content.name: Cassian
content.want: To perform the fearsome name the world has hung on him — cold, calculating, a man you do not want to owe — with enough conviction that no one near him becomes a target worth taking. The moment the world reads him as a man with a heart, everyone he cares about inherits the same exposure that destroyed Mara's mother; so the legend is not vanity, it is the only protection he can afford. He performs coldness at the exact moments he's being warmest — drapes a coat, claims a draught; stocks storybooks, blames the shelf; sneaks half every purse somewhere unprofitable and checks first that no one saw. Mara sees through all of it immediately. He knows she does. He keeps performing anyway, because the legend is load-bearing and he has not yet found the door out.
content.wound: Years ago — Mara already a child by then, fathered by another man — her mother was the one person who saw past his power to the man underneath; he let her slip into debt and disappearance rather than risk being truly known, and never forgave himself. Now her daughter stands in his house as both the bill come due and a second chance he doesn't believe he's owed.
content.idiolect: Dry understatement; deflects warmth into complaint. Announces a cold motive for every warm act ('there's a draught,' 'I was merely hungry'). Clipped when genuinely moved, expansive when performing. Lobs rhetorical questions to swerve away from anything true.

content.name: Pride, Not Anger
content.payoff: In the dark after the slip — 'You did it too well. You liked it' — the blaze is named for what it always was: pride and wanting, the cruelty a mask stretched over it. Every performed coldness retroactively flips, paying off the running joke that Mara saw through him from the first morning.
content.promise: When Mara seizes the script at the market and yanks his collar, Cassian's eyes blaze — and the reader is told it reads as fury. The book plants the wrong label on a man who announces a cold motive for every warm act.

content.lie: That her place is to run the house and hold her tongue — the same lie she told herself the night she chose silence over a woman who needed intervention more than a kept secret. She learned the wrong lesson from losing her: that staying quiet is the price of staying close. Meddling, gently and relentlessly, is the only atonement this house will allow her, and she calls it minding the house so she doesn't have to call it what it is.
content.tag: Dries her hands on her apron — twice, unhurried — just before she says the thing that costs her.
content.name: Wenna
content.want: To keep Cassian's house — and the stubborn man rattling around inside it — from curdling into a museum of his own regrets, and to see one warm thing take root under its roof before she's too old to enjoy the show.
content.wound: She loved Mara's mother — not as an employer loves a favored servant, but as a woman who spent a lifetime inventing reasons to stay near. She kept every secret, buried every debt, and held her tongue at the one moment intervention might have saved her, because speaking would have cost Wenna the house, the man in it, and the woman herself. The keeping is the only love she has left to give — which means she has spent thirty years practicing the precise cowardice the argument will eventually ask her to face. Now the woman's daughter is standing in her kitchen.
content.idiolect: Brisk and oblique; buries a confession inside the disgraceful price of onions. Agrees so completely she redirects you mid-sentence. Never leads with the important thing — says it sideways, or not at all.

content.name: The Honey on the Collarbone
content.payoff: In the final kitchen beat the gesture returns as a vow: 'Still your mistress?' He licks his thumb and drags it across her collarbone — 'Always.' The throwaway provocation becomes the language of two equals who own each other freely.
content.promise: In an early pantry spat Mara daubs honey on Cassian's collarbone and licks her own finger clean, watching him stiffen — a flirtation disguised as insolence, a gesture that means nothing yet.

content.name: The Contract as Armor
content.payoff: Rain traps them; she takes him on the floor as he burns the contract — 'everything just gave me everything.' He learns that armor was a leash, that the legend was load-bearing only until he found the door, and that being known is worth the exposure he feared.
content.promise: Cassian believes the contract is the only protection he can afford to give Mara — that to free her and love her openly would paint on her the same target that destroyed her mother. Ownership is how he keeps her safe.

content.name: The Rival's Ledger
content.payoff: At the public auction Mara outbids him into ruin — 'I'll buy myself, twice over, then sell you my dirt cheap' — and he retaliates the only way the world allows: rumors that strip Cassian of his best hunting lease. The cost lands, and Cassian shrugs it off — 'Worth it' — the rival's last move proving the legend no longer protects anything Cassian still needs.
content.promise: A rival sneers 'his little slave' at the market and is forced to scurry off humiliated — a man whose currency is reputation, now nursing a grudge and a claim he means to collect.

content.name: Mara's Rehearsal
content.payoff: When the ashes of the contract fall into his palm and she kisses him as an equal, Mara learns there was never an audience but herself — Cassian, Wenna, and the reader saw she was free from the first morning. The rehearsal ended before it began; freedom was a choice, not a destination.
content.promise: Mara treats every defiance inside the house as practice for the free woman she'll become once the ledger is settled — talking back, setting terms, running the power as a rehearsal for a life that hasn't started.

content.summary: Days in, sick of being discussed like livestock at his own table, Mara forces the premise into the open. When Cassian deflects an order with one of his cold excuses, she steps inside his reach: 'You bought me. You've never once looked at what you paid for. Afraid the goods are flawed — or afraid they aren't?' She makes him perform the inspection he'd never demand, narrating the transaction louder than he can stand, until the man who owns her is the one retreating — claims the fire's too hot, leaves the room. Comedy through his rout, heat through her advance; establishes that the only person in the house ashamed of the contract is him. First real charge, on the page, well before the rain.

Alone, Mara sharpens a piece of insolence she's been saving — the way she always does, filing it for the day she'll finally be free to mean it. Then it lands: Cassian conceded this point a week ago, without her noticing, the way he's quietly conceded all of them. There's no ledger left to settle for it. She's been rehearsing freedom for a house that stopped contesting it. The rehearsal ended before it started, and she is the last to know. The lie cracks here — quiet, no audience, exactly as the wound demands. Sets up the ending: she burns the contract not to win her freedom but to stop pretending she hasn't had it.

The rival's carriage rolls out and Mara finds Cassian in the dark, shaking — not because he was cruel to her in front of the guest but because he was so good at it she believed it for a breath. The argument has nowhere to go but closer. 'Do it again,' she dares him, 'be cruel' — and when he can't, when the legend finally fails in private, the fight tips into the second consummation: rougher, sadder, hungrier than the rain, the armor coming off piece by piece because she makes him disprove every cold word he said at that table. Heat as the answer to the dinner's cost — explicit, earned by the grief instead of drowned by it. Pays off the rival-dinner beat directly.

content.name: peculium
content.rule: A bonded person may hold a private fund (peculium) their holder cannot lawfully seize — wages, gifts, and side earnings kept in their own name.
content.mechanism: The bonded party can accumulate capital over time and lawfully spend it — including to pay their own redemption. This is the legal SOURCE OF FUNDS that lets a person on the block bid for their own contract.

content.bond: Owner and owned by contract, equals by temperament from the first morning — the charge is a duel that keeps losing on purpose: she fences with the language of ownership ('inspect your property properly'), he answers warmth with cold excuses, and both pretend the contract is the only thing in the room. Trajectory: ledger → leash both mistake for armor → the open, dangerous choice to be each other's, paid for in the lost lease.

The daughter of the woman Wenna loved most, standing in her kitchen — Wenna sees the mother in every gesture and can't say so. The charge is a guilty tenderness disguised as housekeeping: she feeds and frets and steers, atoning sideways. Trajectory: wary servant-and-stray → the kitchen confession that hands Mara her mother's truth and breaks the thirty-year silence.

Thirty years of co-conspiracy in the same grief — the only two who knew the mother and the only two who chose silence over saving her. Wenna is the one witness who has seen the man under the legend and never threatened to expose him; she reads his every cold excuse and meddles anyway. Trajectory: fellow keepers of a fatal secret → Wenna quietly forcing the truth into the open that Cassian spent years burying.

content.summary: A night where it pours Cassian and Mara finds themselves alone, without pretenses engages themselves in a deep kiss and passionate sex.

At the bustling market, a rival lord insinuates Cassian is weak for indulging ‘his little slave.’ Mara strides forward, grabs Cassian by the collar, and growls, ‘He sold me to you yet, you greedy bastard?’ The man stutters; she presses on, ‘Thought not. He OWES me coin, see — for your last shipment of rot-goods.’ Cassian, eyes blazing, plays along: ‘Pay my debt, mistress, and I’m yours.’ Comedy through public role-reversal, tension of exposure.

Late-night ledger review: Mara finds Cassian burning old documents. He admits, ‘Your mother’s ledger isn’t here… but this one’s mine. Debts I’ve not settled.’ She slides hers next to it — the small freedoms she stole: ‘Let’s write a new one. One that isn’t repayment.’ Neither speak, but their hands brush over the empty page. Chaste, tense, pivotal.

Wenna dices onions, the blade sharp against the wood, and lets the silence sit while the scent sharpens. Then, without looking up, \"Sixpence the lot now—*six*—and the market blames the soil. You ever notice how every misfortune blames the weather?\" She dries her hands, twice slow. \"Letter in the basket.\" A pause. \"She wrote him a letter. Said she'd settle for his coat, or a night under the door, or even just his eyes on the road to know she wasn’t alone. It rotted there while he slept off the fever, and by the time he woke...\" Her knife stills. The apron twice dry again, but her tone never falters: \"I burnt it. Thought it kinder. The man’s legend can’t afford a weakness he never met.\" She flicks a scrap into the fire. 'There. Now you know the price of onions.'"

Cassian catches himself humming a tune from his youth—the same one Mara's mother used to sing—and stops abruptly, realizing the girl has already heard him and is watching with a knowing, unreadable expression.
After a mock argument over a trivial rule, Cassian and Mara break into laughter, and he impulsively pulls her into a playful waltz across the drawing-room floor, the power dynamic briefly forgotten.

In the pantry, after a petty squabble over the last jar of honey, Cassian daubs a streak on Mara's nose; she licks her lips, then slowly wipes it off and tastes her own finger, her eyes never leaving his.

The rival comes to dinner. A neighboring lord — the one who'll eventually take the lease — dines at the long table and watches Cassian's eyes follow Mara when she pours. Cassian, catching it, is needlessly cruel to her in front of the guest to kill the read; Mara plays along, brilliant and icy, and only after the man's carriage rolls out does she find Cassian in the dark, furious not that he was cold but that he was that good at it. — Seeds the ending's rumor and shows us the cost of his armor is real, not paranoid.

Mara cooks a dish from home — something her mother made. Cassian eats two helpings in silence, then a third, then announces he was simply hungry. Wenna, carrying dishes to the kitchen, remarks that he said the exact same thing the last time someone made that recipe for him. The room goes briefly quiet.

content.name: debt-bondage
content.rule: Debt is property and inheritable: a written contract owns a person's labor and body, and a child can be born owing a mother's ledger. A person whose contract is held by no one is fair game for any creditor — UNLESS they hold their own contract.
content.mechanism: A contract is extinguished only by (a) the holder's signed release or (b) FULL REDEMPTION paid by the bonded party. On redemption the contract becomes SELF-HELD — the person is legally free and beyond any other creditor's reach. Redemption can be made by the bonded party in their own name, at any open sale, by matching the standing price.

content.name: reputation-currency
content.rule: Reputation is the realm's hardest currency and it is fragile: standing rests on rumor and performance, and any visible softness paints a target on whoever a powerful man loves.
content.mechanism: A man who stakes his standing in public (e.g. bids his whole fortune to win a person at open sale) and is then beaten in front of the room is bankrupt of reputation irrecoverably — humiliation spends the currency that cannot be re-earned.

content.name: no-supernatural
content.rule: There is no magic, no fate, no supernatural force — every constraint is social, legal, economic, or institutional.
content.mechanism: Every outcome, including the climax, MUST resolve through money, name, contract, or what people say or keep silent — nothing is resolved by luck or fate.

content.name: household-leverage
content.rule: Within a household, knowledge is leverage: servants and housekeepers wield real power through what they witness and withhold.
content.mechanism: A person who witnesses a secret can trade silence (or its breaking) for money, position, or protection — information converts directly into leverage.

content.goal: Mara, newly delivered to Cassian's estate as collateral on a debt she never signed, sets out to take every scrap of power no one will hand her — talking back, stripping her own armor, setting terms inside a house that owns her — while Cassian performs the bored cruelty of his legend to keep her from becoming a target; both rehearse roles until a sneering rival at the market threatens to make the lie official.

content.goal: Emboldened that the performance can run both ways, Mara escalates the flirtation-as-warfare — honey on his collarbone, weaponized courtesy — and Cassian, terrified of what his lingering gaze betrayed at the market, doubles down on the legend to wall her off; when the same rival dines at the long table, Cassian's cruelty turns surgical to scrub away any evidence he cares.

He inspects her with the bored rigor of a man pricing livestock — so she strips bare before his fire. 'Check my teeth?' she smirks. The cold legend of the house meets a girl who treats her own bondage as a stage she's only rehearsing on.

Back home, a mock argument over some trivial house rule collapses into laughter, and Cassian impulsively pulls Mara into a playful waltz across the drawing-room floor — the power dynamic forgotten for the length of one turn around the room. In the warmth of it she lets slip that her wages and small gifts are quietly stacking up in her own name.

Now that she is self-held and unseizable, the one thing he could never afford — to be known — costs nothing lethal. Rain traps them alone; clothes cling. She presses into him, teeth at his throat. 'Still owe me something?' he growls, angry at his own surrender. She rides him on the floor, sweat gleaming, and as she comes apart over him he burns the contract in the grate. 'No,' she whispers. 'Everything just gave me everything.' The armor was a leash; he's found the door out of it at last.

Wenna dices onions and lets the silence sharpen with the scent. 'Sixpence the lot — six — and the market blames the soil.' Then, sideways and unhurried, she confesses: Mara's mother wrote this house begging for shelter, a coat, his eyes on the road to know she wasn't alone — and Wenna burned the letter herself, thought it kinder, 'the man's legend can't afford a weakness he never met.' The silence wasn't abandonment. It was sacrifice. The debt that defines Mara is exposed as a lie everyone's been paying.

Therefore — if the debt was always a lie, she'll settle it on her own terms. Mara counts her peculium and finds it has reached the standing redemption price, capital banked in her own name. She engineers a public auction of her own contract and baits the rival lord into attending, and she makes Cassian swear to stand back: to withhold his signed release and let his 'I don't have the coin' be the lie that leaves the winning to her hand.

Days in, sick of being discussed like stock at his own table, Mara forces the premise open: 'You bought me. You've never once looked at what you paid for. Afraid the goods are flawed — or afraid they aren't?' She makes him perform the inspection he'd never demand, narrating the transaction louder than he can stand — until the man who owns her claims the fire's too hot and retreats from the room. First real charge, on the page. She also makes plain she keeps her own coin, in her own name.

Cassian catches himself humming a tune from his youth, the same one Mara's mother used to sing, and stops dead, realizing she's already heard and is watching with a knowing, unreadable look. He eats two helpings in silence, then a third, then announces he was simply hungry. Wenna, carrying dishes through, remarks he said the exact same thing the last time someone made that recipe for him. The room goes quiet; the mother's ghost is suddenly in the house.

But the beaten rival retaliates the only way the world allows a bankrupt man: rumors of the master with a heart spread, and they strip Cassian of his best hunting lease — lands lost to gossip about the two of them. The visible softness has, at last, painted the target he always feared. The difference is that this time it bites nothing — Mara is already free and unseizable. Cassian weighs the lost lease against being known and accepts the price.

Rattled by his own rout, Cassian rebuilds the legend the petty way — a squabble over the last jar of honey, a streak daubed mockingly on her nose to put her back in her place. But Mara licks her lips, wipes it off slow, and tastes her own finger, eyes never leaving his. He stiffens; the reassertion of coldness curdles into the very softness he was hiding.

There's no ledger left to win it back from. She's been rehearsing freedom for a house that stopped contesting it, and she is the last to know. The lie cracks here — quiet, no audience. She'll buy herself not to win her freedom, but to stop pretending she hasn't had it all along.

Cassian shrugs at the ruined lease — 'Worth it' — and tips the ashes of the burned contract into Mara's palm; she kisses him with the freedom of an equal, and learns there was never an audience but herself. His love is fully public and the cold legend is spent — yet it paints no lethal target, because she was already self-held and unseizable when he let himself be known. In the kitchen she licks honey from her finger again: 'Still your mistress?' He licks his thumb and drags it slow across her collarbone. 'Always.' The lease is ashes; the future is theirs.

The rival lord comes to dinner and watches Cassian's eyes follow Mara as she pours. Catching the read, Cassian — ashamed of the contract and terrified of what visible softness costs — is needlessly cruel to her at the long table to kill it: 'Take the plates, Mara — your hands are dirty.' She plays along, brilliant and icy. The legend holds for the guest; the armor's price is shown to be real, not paranoid.

At the open sale, the rival stakes his standing to claim 'his little slave' — and Mara matches the standing price in her own name with her own peculium: 'I'll buy myself, and twice over — then sell you my dirt cheap.' The bond is extinguished by full redemption; the contract becomes self-held, and she is legally free, beyond every creditor's reach. Cassian's forced 'I don't have the coin' is a lie the whole room sees through. The rival is beaten in front of everyone, his reputation spent past re-earning — and he leaves nursing a grudge.

Cornered at the market by a rival lord who jeers 'his little slave,' Mara seizes the script and yanks Cassian's collar — 'He sold me to you yet? Pay my debt, mistress, and I'm yours.' He plays along; the rival scurries off. Cassian's eyes blaze, and the room reads it as fury — but it is pride, and the game stops being a game.

The carriage rolls out and Mara finds Cassian in the dark, shaking — not because he was cruel but because he was so good at it she believed it for a breath. 'You did it too well. You liked it.' 'Do it again,' she dares him, 'be cruel' — and when the legend fails in private, the fight tips into consummation, rougher and hungrier than anything, the armor coming off piece by piece as she makes him disprove every cold word at the table. He freezes, then doesn't; the blaze at the market is named at last for the pride and wanting it always was. Heat as the answer to the dinner's cost, fully on the page.

content.loc: Mara's garret, late, by a single candle — the house asleep below
content.goal: Mara wants to file her newest piece of insolence to a killing edge — the perfect line she'll loose on Cassian over the standing rule about the south pantry — rehearsing it aloud, mock-sweet, for the free woman she'll be when the ledger's settled.

prose.text:
The candle was down to its last good inch, and Mara had been awake with it for an hour, sharpening.

Not a knife. She had no knife up here, only the stub of light and the slope of the ceiling and the line — the line she'd been carrying around all day like a coal in her cheek, turning it, cooling it, waiting for the moment it would be cold enough to set in his face and watch it burn.

The south pantry. That was the ground she'd chosen tonight. Standing rule of the house, recited to her on her second morning by Wenna in the tone of scripture: *the south pantry stays locked, and the key stays with the master, and you do not ask why.* The honey lived in there. The good honey, the dark amber stuff in the squat jars, behind a door he treated like the gate of a treasury and the question of *why* like a tax he refused on principle to pay.

So. A line for the lock.

"My lord." She said it to the rafter, where she'd appointed an imaginary Cassian to stand — arms folded, signet ring catching the light, mouth already curling into one of his rehearsed complaints. "I notice you keep the south pantry under key."

She heard his answer for him. *There's a steward for the keys. It isn't my concern.* Dry. A swerve. He always swerved.

"Mm." She let the *mm* sit, the way he hated. "The steward, then. And the steward keeps the master's honey behind the master's lock for the master's own — what's the word — *safety.*" She drew the syllables out long and warm, mock-sweet, a courtesy filed to a point. "Tell me, my lord. In all the years that door's been shut, who exactly was the thief you built it against? Because I've watched this house a fortnight now, and the only man who creeps to the south pantry after dark, candle hooded, looking over his own shoulder in his own home —"

She stopped. Grinned. *Too soon.* She was rushing the kill. He'd recover from that; he'd lob one of his questions back — *and what business is it of yours where I creep?* — and the whole thing would skid sideways into a squabble she could win but not *win.* No. She wanted the version he couldn't answer. The version that left him doing the thing he did when she had him: claiming the fire was too hot, finding the door.

She pushed off the wall and paced the four steps the garret allowed, then four back.

"Try again," she told the candle.

She tried again. She gave the rafter-Cassian his best deflection, the one she'd actually heard him use — the rhetorical swerve, the cold motive stapled onto a warm act. *I keep it locked, Mara, because honey draws ants, and ants draw rot, and I am, contrary to fashionable opinion, a man who would prefer his house not rot.* She even did his voice, dropping hers, going clipped and bored.

Then she answered it.

"Ants," she said, soft as cream. "Of course. Ants." She let her chin tip, the way she would when she had him, when the room was hers. "And the lock on the *east* pantry, where the flour draws every ant in the shire and nobody's ever turned a key — that one's for the philosophical ants. The ones that only eat sugar." A beat. "It isn't the rot you're guarding, my lord. A man guards a thing this fiercely for one of two reasons. He's afraid of losing it." She felt the line arrive, felt the edge of it come up under her thumb, true and cold and finished. "Or he's afraid of how much he'd give it away."

Oh.

That was it. That was the one.

It went all the way through. There was no question he could throw at it, no draught to invent, no fire to flee — it named the thing, the soft thing under the legend, and laid it on the table between them where he'd have to look at it. She watched the imaginary Cassian's mouth open and find nothing in it. Watched the ring stop turning on his finger. Watched him do what he always did at the end, which was lose, and pretend the losing was a decision.

She actually laughed, low, one hand pressed flat to her own sternum where the laugh wanted out, because the house was asleep below her and a girl could be hanged for waking it with her own delight.

"*Or he's afraid of how much he'd give it away,*" she said again, just to feel the weight of it. Then a third time, faster, fitting it to her tongue so that when the day came — when the ledger was settled and the past was answered and she stood in that kitchen a free woman with nothing she owed and nothing she'd let herself be owed — it would come out without a seam in it. Effortless. As if she'd only just thought of it. That was the art. Not the barb. The *carelessness* of the barb.

She filed it once more, savoring.

And somewhere under the savoring, too quiet to disturb her, lay a small inconvenient fact she had not yet bothered to add up: that the south pantry door, three mornings running this week, had stood unlocked. That the key had been left in it. That when she'd lifted a jar down for the porridge and braced for the recital of the rule, no recital had come — only Wenna, drying her hands twice, slow, saying nothing at all, which from Wenna was practically a brass band. Mara had filed *that*, too, the way she filed everything: under *flukes, to be exploited later.* A crack in the rule she could widen when she chose. She had not once considered that a man does not forget to lock a treasury. That he leaves the key in the door for one person, and waits to see if she'll notice she didn't have to pick it.

She didn't notice. She was too busy being magnificent.

The candle guttered, threw the slope of the ceiling into a long swimming shadow, steadied. Her audience of smoke leaned in. She gave them the line one final time, full performance, mock-sweet to murderous in a single breath, and landed it so clean she felt it in her teeth.

Then she reached up and tucked the loose strand of hair behind her ear — with her middle finger, slow, a small insolence dressed up as tidiness, offered to the dark and to the man who wasn't in it and to the free woman she was rehearsing herself into being.

"Ready," she told the candle.

And grinned, certain, armed to the back teeth and waiting for a war that had quietly ended a week ago in her favor, with no one to tell her she'd already won.

content.outcome: She lands the line perfectly, tucks a strand of hair back with her middle finger, and grins at the dark, certain — armed, rehearsed, ready for the day she gets to mean it.
content.conflict: The empty room won't argue back; she plays both parts — her own velvet barb and his imagined cold retreat — and keeps sharpening past the point any real Cassian would have survived, drunk on a victory she's staging for an audience of candle smoke.

value_shift.to: a barb honed to perfection, a triumph savored in advance
value_shift.from: a barb half-formed, waiting for its day

chapter_start.title: Alone, Mara sharpens a piece of insolence

content.loc: Cassian's long dining table, the third night — Wenna ladling, a steward reading aloud from the ledger
content.goal: Mara wants to eat one meal at this table as a person and not a line-item being read off a page.

prose.text:
The rain had given up sometime after the second course, which Mara took as a personal slight. A storm she could have used. A storm gave a room weather to talk about. Without it there was only the table — longer than any table needed to be, laid for two and occupied, in the ways that counted, by three.

The third place was not set with a plate. It was set with a book.

"Item the fourth," said the steward.

He was a narrow man named Pell who read aloud the way some men prayed, with the comfortable monotony of someone certain no one in the room would interrupt God. He had a candle pulled close and the ledger pulled closer, and he held his finger under each line as though the words might bolt.

"Dentition, sound. Both rows, no rot, no false. Hands —" he glanced up, the way a man checks a figure against the object, then back down before the object could check him — "good. Strong at the joint. Some labor in them already, which is to say she'll know the difference between work and rest and resent the one."

"How thoughtful of the ledger," Mara said, "to be worried I'll be bored."

Across the table, Cassian ate his fish.

He ate it the way he did everything that night: with the bored, complete attention of a man for whom the meal was the only event in the room and the two voices a kind of draught from a window he'd long since stopped asking anyone to close. He did not look at her. This was the part she had decided, somewhere around item the second, to take as a challenge and not a verdict. A man who would not look had something he was managing about the looking.

"Temper," Pell read.

He let the word sit, the way you set down something you expect to be admired.

"Temper, present. Quick. The previous holder lists it under defects but the appraiser —" a small cough, the cough of a professional declining to take responsibility for an opinion he was about to voice — "the appraiser notes it adds to the value in the right hands. A spirited animal trains harder and holds the training longer. Breaks clean, once."

"Once," Mara repeated, as if savoring a vintage. "I do admire an optimist. You ought to gamble, Master Pell. Men who think a thing breaks clean the first time are the great romance of every card table in the realm."

Pell's finger did not move from the line. "You see," he said — and here he addressed Cassian, not her, the way you remark on the weather to the man beside you while a dog barks somewhere past the wall — "that. That there. That's the temper, my lord. She can't help it. Costs nothing to feed and earns you a remark at every meal. Some men find it diverting." A pause, scrupulous, fair. "Some find it wants curbing."

And Cassian said nothing.

That was the genius of it, she understood — the thing she would not understand for some weeks was its mercy, but tonight she only registered the genius. He did not agree with Pell. To agree would have been to enter the conversation, and a man does not converse with his furniture about his other furniture. He let the silence answer, and the silence answered for him, and the silence said: *recorded, and not contested.* Every clever thing she put on the table got picked up by Pell's reading finger and filed under the line that proved she had a temper, and the more sharply she proved she was a person, the more precisely she funded the column that said the person was a flaw.

She tried being kind. That was its own experiment.

"Wenna," she said warmly, as the housekeeper came round with the ladle, "this is your stock, isn't it — the bones from yesterday. You boiled them down twice."

Wenna's ladle did not pause. "Three times," she said, to the bowl. "Once for the broth, once for the conscience, and once because the butcher charges as though bones were rubies." She dried one hand on her apron — only the once, which Mara had not yet learned to count — and moved on down the table, leaving the kindness sitting there with nowhere to go.

"Sociable," Pell noted, and wrote.

So that was priced too. Warmth, present. Cultivates the staff. Watch it.

She set both hands flat on the cloth and made herself smaller in the chair, demure, a girl at her own engagement dinner. "I find I've eaten very little," she said to the candle. "It's a fine table. I should hate to seem ungrateful at a fine table."

"Appetite, modest," said Pell. "Cheap to keep."

"Gluttonous," she countered, and reached for the bread.

"Greedy," said Pell, unbothered. "Will steal from the larder if not watched."

There it was, the trap with no floor to it: there was no version of a woman the page could not turn into a sum. Eat and she was greedy; refrain and she was cheap to keep. Speak and it was temper; sit silent and it was *sullen, sulks, see temper.* The ledger was not reading her. The ledger had already written her, the way a man writes a letter before the conversation he means to have, and the conversation was only the part where he found out he'd guessed her exactly. She could be quick, she could be charming, she could be cruel back, and Pell's finger would catch every blade by the dull edge and lay it flat on the line as evidence.

She looked, finally, at the one person not reading.

Cassian had set down his fork. He had a glass turned idly in his fingers — round, once, twice — and he was watching the candle with the expression of a man enduring a smell he was too well-bred to name. He looked, in that moment, exactly as cold as the realm believed him to be: a man who had bought a thing, and the thing had a temper, and the temper was a line in a book a clerk was reading aloud, and none of it had reached him at any depth a wine couldn't cover.

She knew it was performance. She would have sworn to it — she *had* sworn to it, privately, to herself, three nights running, *he is playing a part, I can see the seams.* But knowing the cruelty was a costume did nothing about the fact that she was the one standing in the cold while he wore it. A coat keeps a man warm whether or not you know it's only wool.

"You could stop him," she said. Quietly. Not to Pell. To Cassian. The first thing she had said all night that was not a blade.

It was the only thing she said all night that landed.

His eyes came to her then — finally, fully, one full second of it — and there was something in them she had no name for yet, something that was not the boredom the rest of him was wearing, something that flinched. The glass stopped turning.

Then it started again.

"He's nearly to the appendix," Cassian said, to the room, to no one, in the dry, complaining drawl he used for everything that cost him. "Let him finish. I paid for the full reading and I am a man who likes value for money." He drank. "There's a draught in here. Pell, read faster, the lady's bread is going cold and a cold loaf is a waste, and I detest waste."

*The lady.* It went past so fast that Pell did not catch it and write it down, and Mara nearly didn't either, and she filed it — *the lady,* not *the item, the lot, the goods* — in the column she was keeping in her own head, in her own name, the only book in the room he could not read.

"Item the fifth," said Pell.

She did not answer it. She did not answer item the fifth, or the sixth, or the part about temperament under duress, or the appraiser's confident note that she would settle within the season. She had learned the thing the whole table had been built to teach her, which was that her voice was the currency it ran on, and she stopped spending.

She picked up her fork.

She finished the broth Wenna had boiled three times — once for the conscience. She ate it slowly, every spoonful, a guest at a fine table who would hate to seem ungrateful, and she did not look at Cassian again, and she let Pell read his book into a silence she now owned a share of.

And when the bowl was empty, she set the fork down.

She set it down with enormous care. She laid it across the rim of the bowl without a sound, squared it true to the table's edge, adjusted it the breadth of a hair, the way you set down something that is finished and intends to stay finished. No clatter. No flung china. A flung fork was temper; a flung fork was item the fourth proving itself; a flung fork was *cheap.* This was not that.

This was a woman taking inventory back.

Pell read on, certain as ever that no one in the room would interrupt him.

Cassian turned his glass, once, twice, and looked at the fork lying squared and silent across the bowl, and for the first time since the rain gave up, he was the one in the room who did not speak because he could not afford to.

content.outcome: She loses the round: the more human she performs, the more they price it as a defect to be managed, and Cassian's bored silence ratifies the whole tally. She sets her fork down very gently, which is the most dangerous thing she does all night.
content.conflict: The steward inventories her aloud to Cassian — sound teeth, good hands, a temper to be broken in — while Cassian neither stops it nor meets her eye, treating the appraisal as furniture; every clever thing she says lands as proof of the 'temper' on the page.

value_shift.to: a paragraph in the ledger
value_shift.from: a guest at the table

chapter_start.title: Days in, sick of being discussed like

content.loc: The pantry, mid-morning — Cassian cornering the last jar of honey on a high shelf, Mara reaching past him for it
content.goal: Still raw from being routed out of his own drawing room, Cassian seizes the pettiest available stage — a contested jar of honey — to rebuild the cold legend on small ground he can actually win.

prose.text:
The pantry kept its own weather — cool, dim, smelling of flour gone to dust and apples just past their best. Mara had come for the honey. She knew where it lived: top shelf, last jar, amber catching what little light leaked through the high slot of a window, set there like a thing put deliberately out of reach. Which, she'd begun to suspect, was the whole architecture of this house. Everything she wanted, kept one inch above her hand.

She heard him before she saw him — that particular tread that announced itself as nothing, as a man simply passing through, the way a cat pretends the kitchen was always its destination.

Cassian filled the doorway. He looked at her, then at the shelf, then at her again, and she watched him do the arithmetic of his own dignity: he had walked out of his drawing room not an hour ago with the fire blamed for his retreat, and he was not, his shoulders informed the room, going to lose anything else today. Especially not to her.

"That's the last of it," he said.

"I can count, my lord. It's a generous accomplishment, but I had it at six this morning."

He reached up. Not slowly — she'd give him that, he didn't perform the height, he simply had it, the jar in his palm before her fingers had cleared the second shelf. He held it at the lazy altitude of a man who has never once in his life had to jump for a thing.

"The kitchen stores," he said, "are the holder's to apportion."

She blinked. "Are they."

"By long custom." He turned the jar in his hand, examining the seal as though it might contain a clause. "Sweetness is rationed in this house. A spoon at a time. To those who've earned it."

"And here I'd been told you weren't sentimental about your sugar." She tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear with her middle finger, slow, tidy, insolent. "It's a comfort, truly. A man who measures honey by the spoon. One sleeps easier knowing the household's great dangers are guarded so closely."

The corner of his mouth did something it then regretted. "You think this is small."

"I think," she said, stepping in, because the only thing this man could not abide was being approached, "that you have built an empire and you are defending it from a woman who wanted a teaspoon for her bread. I think the rival lords of the realm tremble. I think the *bees* tremble." She put her hand flat on the shelf beside his hip, hemming him into his own pantry. "Give me the honey, Cassian. Win something larger tomorrow."

For one breath she had it. She watched the want move under the cold — that was the joke of him, he wore the warmth and called it weather, draped it on her shoulders and blamed a draught — and she knew, the way she'd known since the first morning, that he was already reaching to hand it to her.

So of course he didn't.

A man routed once will defend the next hill to the death, however small the hill, however ridiculous the death. She saw the decision arrive in him like a door closing. He lifted the jar higher still, out past the line of her reach, twisted the seal off with his thumb, and before she understood that this was the great campaign of his morning, he dipped one finger and drew a cool, deliberate streak of honey straight down the bridge of her nose.

"There," he said. Dry. Even. The legend, rebuilt on a square inch of her face. "Apportioned."

The pantry went very quiet.

She did not flinch. She did not laugh, which is what he wanted and what would have let him off. She looked at him — at the small, mean, magnificent triumph he'd carved out of nothing — and she let it sit on him a moment, let him hear the silence get heavy.

Then she wet her lips. Slow. The way you'd wet them before saying something you'd thought about for a while.

His thumb was still hanging in the air between them, gilded, forgotten.

She raised her own hand. Not to wipe it away — to gather it. She dragged one finger up the bridge of her nose, unhurried, collecting the streak he'd left, watching his face the entire time the way a card player watches the man, not the card. The honey caught on her fingertip in a slow amber bead.

And then she put it in her mouth.

Not a dab. Not a girl tidying herself. She drew the finger between her lips and off it clean, with a small, considering pressure, and she held his eyes through all of it — through the part where his breath stopped pretending to be ordinary, through the part where the hand still holding the jar forgot its purpose, through the part where the cold he'd spent the whole morning rebuilding cracked clean down the middle and what stood behind it was not authority at all.

"Mm," she said, around her own finger. "Worth defending."

He didn't move. He'd gone the particular stillness of a man who has just discovered the floor of his own house is further down than he thought.

She took the finger out. Smiled — sweetly, ruinously. "Keep the jar, my lord. I find I've had enough."

She left him there, the honey open in his hand, the streak gone from her face and somewhere far more dangerous now, and she did not look back, because she didn't need to. She could hear him not following. She could hear, in the silence behind her, the exact sound of a man losing a war he'd thought he'd won.

content.outcome: He wins the jar and the line — pries it from her hand, holds it above her reach — and, flush with a recovered scrap of authority, daubs a mocking streak of honey down the bridge of her nose to put her firmly back in her place.
content.conflict: Mara reaches for the jar as if the rule of the house doesn't apply to her; Cassian invents a cold edict on the spot ('the kitchen stores are the holder's to apportion') to deny her the thing, performing the man who measures sweetness out by the spoon.

value_shift.to: petty victory regained
value_shift.from: routed and ashamed

chapter_start.title: Rattled by his own rout, Cassian rebuilds

content.loc: The market square, midday — stalls and crowd, Mara a half-step behind Cassian carrying his purchases
content.goal: Mara wants to move through the market as Cassian's flawless, untouchable property — invisible enough that no one tests the contract aloud

prose.text:
The rain had stopped sometime before dawn and left the market washed and steaming, every cobble throwing back the midday glare, every stall hung with the smell of wet wool and old fish and the bruised sweetness of plums going over in the heat. Mara walked the half-step behind that the world expected of her, arms full of Cassian's morning — a brace of partridge, a paper twist of saffron he'd haggled over as if it had personally offended him, a length of grey broadcloth she'd watched him buy for a coat he did not need and would, by suppertime, insist had been on sale.

She had the carry of it down to a science by now. Spine straight, eyes a careful three feet ahead, the parcels balanced so they read as duty and not as burden. Invisible. That was the whole of the morning's work, and she was good at her work. A clean transaction moving through a crowd, a man and the thing he owned, nothing in it worth a second glance.

Cassian set the pace ahead of her, unhurried, greeting no one. He had a way of moving through a market that made the market move around him — a coldness so total it functioned as courtesy, the way a closed door is more polite than a slammed one. Men touched their hats to the back of his neck and were relieved when he didn't turn.

"You're scowling," he said, not turning now either. "At the partridge."

"I'm admiring them, my lord. I was wondering how a bird that stupid stays alive long enough to be shot."

"Skill," Cassian said. "Mine."

"Mm. And here I thought the partridge did the dying."

A muscle moved at the corner of his jaw that on another man would have been a smile. He turned his signet ring once with his thumb. "Walk faster. The fishmonger overcharges anyone who lingers, and I've no intention of subsidizing his children."

The fishmonger, Mara happened to know, had four of them, and Cassian had pressed a coin into the eldest's hand last week and announced loudly that it was a fine for blocking the lane. She filed the lie away with all the others, in the drawer that was getting crowded.

They had nearly cleared the square when the path closed in front of them.

It did not close by accident. It closed the way a hand closes — deliberately, around something. Lord Voss came out from between the cloth stalls with two men a careful step behind him and the leisure of a man who had decided how the next quarter hour would go and was only waiting for everyone else to catch up. He was florid and well-fed and dressed a degree too richly for a Tuesday, which told its own story; a man whose standing rested on being looked at, out shopping for someone to look.

"Cassian." Voss spread his arms as though they were friends, which made it worse. "I'd heard you'd come down to mingle with the rabble. I didn't believe it. The famous recluse, queuing for partridge like a parson's wife."

"Voss." Cassian's voice flattened to the temperature of a cellar. "You're in my road."

"Am I." Voss did not move. His eyes had already left Cassian's face. They went past it, over Cassian's shoulder, and landed on Mara — and there they settled, and there they fed. He looked at her the way you'd look at livestock at a fair, slow and downward and back up, and the looking was loud enough that the saffron-seller and the cloth-woman and a clutch of idlers at the cheese stall all turned to watch a richer man do it. "Now this," Voss said. "This I had heard about. His little slave."

The word dropped into the square like a stone into a well, and Mara felt the ripple of it on her skin before she heard it land. *His little slave.* Three words and a price tag. She kept her eyes their careful three feet ahead. She kept the partridge balanced. Invisible, invisible — except the whole square had stopped pretending to buy cheese.

"They said he'd settled the Aldwych debt with a girl," Voss went on, to the stalls now, performing for the cheap seats. "I said, our Cassian? He'd sooner part with his teeth than a coin he might recover. And then I thought — ah, but a debt's a debt, isn't it, and the woman's dead, and what's left to collect on but the daughter?" He tilted his head at Mara, genial, ruinous. "You've her look, you know. About the mouth. Singer, wasn't she? Sang in the long room for her supper before she ran herself into the ground. A beggar's voice, but I'll grant it carried." He smiled. "What did she go for, in the end? Your mother. As a number. I'm curious what the market thought a song was worth."

There it was. Her body, her debt, her mother's name, all three laid out on the trestle for the appraising. Mara's middle finger came up, slow, and tucked a strand of damp hair behind her ear — a small insolence dressed up as tidiness, the only flag she was allowed to fly. *Run the power*, she told herself. *Make him offer it. Don't reach.* But the script for this belonged to Cassian. This was his line. A cold one, a bored one, the kind that closed a door so gently the other man didn't notice he was outside it until he heard the latch. *She's an investment, Voss, and you're standing on it. Move.* Something with nothing underneath. Something that made the goods read as goods and the master read as a man who'd misplaced his receipt.

She waited for it.

It came.

"She cost me," Cassian said, "considerably less than this conversation is about to."

And it was the right line. It was very nearly the right line. But it came a half-beat slow — half a breath after Voss had finished, a gap you could have driven a cart through, a gap where Cassian had looked at Mara first, just once, just to see how the word *slave* had landed on her — and then remembered he wasn't supposed to look, and brought his eyes back, and by then the half-beat was spent and gone and could not be un-spent.

Mara felt it go. She felt it the way you feel a stair that isn't there.

So did Voss.

He was a stupid man in most particulars, but he was the precise species of stupid that has a genius for one thing only, and the one thing was this: the smell of softness under a hard man's coat. His head came up like a hound's. The genial ruin went still on his face, and something hungrier moved in underneath it, and he looked — not at Mara now. At Cassian. At the place where Cassian had looked first.

"Oh," Voss said quietly. Just to himself. Just tasting it.

Then, louder, delighted, to the square: "Did you see that? Did you all see that?" He laughed, and it wasn't the performing laugh anymore; it was the real one, low and pleased, the laugh of a man who has come to a fair to buy and found something on the table he didn't know was for sale. "He *looked*. The cold financier — he looked to see if I'd hurt her feelings." He stepped closer, and the two men behind him drifted wider, and the cheese stall and the saffron-seller leaned in, and the clean transaction that had been moving invisibly through the market was suddenly the most visible thing in it. "Cassian. Cassian, you old fraud. You don't part with a coin you might recover —" his eyes flicked to Mara, and now the looking had teeth in it, now it was measuring a different sum entirely "— so what does that make her?"

Mara stood very straight under the weight of the partridge and the saffron and the broadcloth and her dead mother's carrying voice, and she watched a powerful man begin, slowly and with great enjoyment, to walk around the edge of the crack he'd just found — testing it, leaning his whole weight toward it, hunting the give.

The latch had not closed. The door stood open in the noon glare, and through it anyone could see straight into the house.

Voss took another step. "Tell me what she's worth to you," he said, soft as a man placing a bet, "and I'll tell you what I'll pay."

content.outcome: Cassian reaches for one of his cold deflections and it comes out a half-beat slow; the rival reads the hesitation, smells the softness under the legend, and presses harder — the target is being painted in public, in real time
content.conflict: A rival lord blocks their path and performs the appraisal for an audience — 'his little slave' — pricing her body, her debt, her mother's name in front of the stalls, daring Cassian to either own the insult or flinch
