prose.text:
The auctioneer's stand had been a butter-cask that morning. Someone had upended it, thrown a board across the top, and now it passed for a place where a person could be sold, which Mara thought said everything worth knowing about the dignity of the proceeding. She stood on it in the good light. She had chosen the hour herself — noon, when the market was thickest, when the fishwives had nothing to do but watch and the grain factors had coin warming in their palms and nowhere yet to spend it. A crowd is a kind of ledger too. She had spent a week learning to read this one.

"One contract," the auctioneer called, squinting at the paper as though the words might rearrange themselves into something less troublesome. "Held against the estate of— ah— against the late debt of one Soraya, transferred and current, the bearer—" He gave up on the bearer. "The standing's been set. Eleven hundred."

Eleven hundred. She knew the figure the way she knew the inside of her own wrist. She had counted to it in the dark more nights than she would ever admit, stacking the peculium coin by coin — the wages, the market commissions Wenna let her keep and pretended not to notice, the half-purses that found their way into her apron from a man who always checked first that no one had seen him do it. Eleven hundred, in her own name, in a strongbox no creditor in the realm could lawfully touch. She had not told a soul she had reached it. She had only sent three invitations.

One of them was here.

Lord Hessit came through the crowd the way a man comes through a crowd he believes he owns — shoulders first, an attendant clearing the path he could perfectly well have cleared himself. He wore the green he wore when he wanted to be seen wearing it. He stopped at the foot of the cask and looked up at her with the particular pleasure of a man collecting on a debt he has watered and tended.

"Eleven hundred," Hessit said, loud, to the auctioneer, but not to the auctioneer. "And I'll thank the market to note who said it first."

The crowd noted. That was the trouble with Hessit — he always made sure the crowd noted. He had a face built for being seen and a name built for being repeated, and he had spent both, just now, in front of everyone, on her. She watched him do it and felt something in her chest go very still and very warm, the way a hand goes still over a card it has been waiting all night to turn.

She found Cassian without meaning to. He stood back where she had asked him to stand, at the edge of the press, turning his signet ring once, twice, his face arranged into the bored, faintly nauseated expression of a man enduring a transaction beneath his notice. Anyone watching would have read a financier resenting an inconvenience. She read the white knuckle on the ring. She read the man not breathing.

*Stand back,* she had told him. *Whatever it costs you, stand back. This one is mine to win or there was never any point.*

He had argued. Of course he had argued — he had offered, that morning, in the gray light, to simply sign the release and be done, to hand her the freedom across the breakfast things like a man passing the salt. And she had nearly let him. That was the worst of it, how nearly she had let him. Then she had understood that to take it from his hand was to spend the next forty years suspecting it had been his to give. So: stand back. Let the room see you have no part in this. Let your purse stay shut and let everyone draw the only conclusion the shut purse allows.

He was standing back. It was costing him something visible. She loved him a little extra for the cost.

"Eleven hundred to the lord in green," the auctioneer announced, relieved to have a name attached to a sum. "Do I hear—"

"Eleven hundred," Mara said.

The word landed in the market like a dropped plate. Heads turned. The auctioneer turned. Even the fishwives, who had seen everything twice, leaned in.

"From the—" The auctioneer looked at the paper, looked at her, looked at the paper. "From the contract."

"From its holder." She let the correction sit. "Which, as of this morning's reckoning, I have the honor to be." She had not raised her voice. She had learned long ago that you never raise your voice at the moment everyone is already listening; you lower it, and make them lean. "Eleven hundred. Matched, in my own name, with my own coin, paid in full." She tilted her head, mock-courteous, the soul of helpfulness. "You'll want to check the figure, sir. I'd hate for anyone to say I came up short in front of so many witnesses."

The auctioneer checked the figure. The whole front of the crowd checked the figure, craning. The peculium was law and the law was plain and the strongbox was real, and a contract matched at standing price by the bonded party in her own name was extinguished where it stood — self-held, paid out, beyond the reach of every creditor breathing, including the one in green who had just told the entire market he meant to hold it.

"It's— " The auctioneer cleared his throat. "It's redemption. It's a full redemption. The bond's— the bond is discharged."

"Discharged," Mara agreed warmly, as if congratulating him on a difficult sum.

Hessit's face had not yet decided what to do. This was the part she had wanted to watch. A man's standing is a thing he carries on the outside, where everyone can see whether he still has it, and Hessit had set his down on a board in front of the whole market and reached for her and closed his hand on air. She could see him understanding it in pieces. The eleven hundred he'd shouted so the crowd would mark it his. The crowd, marking it. The property, declining to be property — not by anyone's mercy, not by Cassian's release, but by her own hand and her own coin, which meant there had never been a lord on earth who could have outbid this. He had staked his name to win a woman who could not be won, and he had done it where it would be remembered, and now the only two roads left to him both ran downhill.

"This is a farce," Hessit said. He chose rage. She had thought he might. "She's a— she was bonded yesterday. Where does a slave find eleven hundred?"

"Where does a lord find it?" she asked pleasantly. "I'm told the methods are remarkably alike. A great deal of standing in front of people, mostly." A snort somewhere to her left — a grain factor, hand over his mouth. She had that one now. She angled toward Hessit, confiding, generous, as if doing him a kindness in front of his friends. "But since you've gone to the trouble of telling everyone here what I'm worth — eleven hundred, you said, and twice you said it — let me return the courtesy. You've a sharp eye for a price, my lord. Truly. It's a rare man who knows exactly what a thing is worth right up until the moment he can't have it."

"You overreach," Hessit said, but quieter now, because he had heard the laugh start to gather and he knew the sound of a market turning the way a sailor knows the sound of a coming wind.

"Do I." She straightened. She let her own purse hang plain at her hip where everyone could see it heavy, and lifted her chin toward the green lord with the warmth of a woman doing arithmetic she enjoys. "Here's the whole of it, then, for the record, since we're keeping one. I've bought myself. At standing price, paid in full, in my own name — so call it eleven hundred for the woman." She paused, exactly long enough. "I'd have paid double and counted it cheap. So that's me bought, and bought again — and with what's left over—" she patted the purse, and the coin in it spoke for her, "—I find I've still the spare to make you an offer, my lord, by way of thanks. I'll sell you yourself. Dirt cheap."

The market broke.

It was not a polite laugh and it was not a kind one. It came up out of the fishwives first and rolled back through the grain factors and the apprentices and the carters until it had the whole square, the great ugly delighted roar a crowd makes when a big man has been made small in front of it and it is permitted, just this once, to enjoy him. Hessit stood in the center of it in his good green. He had bought that laugh himself. He had paid eleven hundred of his own name to set the scene where it could happen, and there was no clerk in the realm who could enter a refund. Reputation is the one coin you cannot pick up off the ground once you've thrown it down and watched it lose. He had thrown it down. It had lost. He would not, she knew — looking at his face, which had stopped deciding and simply gone white — he would not re-earn this. Not at any market, not at any table, not in any year left to him. A man can recover from being hated. There is no recovering from being funny.

His eyes came up and found her, and in them she read the grudge taking root — the slow, patient, expensive grudge of a man who has nothing left to spend but spite, and means to spend it carefully. *Good,* she thought, surprising herself. *Come and collect. There's nothing here you can hold anymore.* He turned. He went the way he had come, except that the crowd did not part for him now; he had to find the gaps himself, green shoulders working through laughter that did not stop until his carriage was well out of the square.

And then it was only the matter of the paper. The auctioneer, flustered and a little gleeful himself, made the marks the law required, and pressed the wax, and held the contract out to her — the same contract she had carried into this house chained to her wrist like a ring nobody had proposed with. She took it. It weighed nothing. She had always thought it would weigh something.

Across the square, Cassian had not moved. He stood at the edge of the press with his purse at his belt — fat, untouched, conspicuously closed — and that was the other confession the market would carry home tonight, the one he had let her wring out of him this morning over the breakfast things. *I don't have the coin,* he had said for the rehearsal, dry as a ledger, *you understand. A man can't be seen squandering eleven hundred on a discharged bond. Bad for the name.* And every soul in this square had watched the realm's coldest purse stay shut while a woman bought herself off the block — watched the man who supposedly owned her decline, with a full purse, to lift a finger to keep her — and not one of them believed it. You could see the not-believing move through the crowd. You could see them glance from his closed purse to her free hands and arrive, every one of them, at the single thing the closed purse could not mean and therefore meant. He had armored himself in indifference and the indifference had come off in their hands like wet paint. He knew it. She watched him know it. He turned the signet ring once, twice, and looked at her across the heads of the people who had just decided what he was, and did not bother, for once, to announce a cold reason for the warm thing on his face.

Mara stepped down off the butter-cask into a market that no longer had any opinion about who she belonged to. The board wobbled under her foot and she let it. She tucked the discharged contract into her bodice with two fingers, and the loose strand of hair behind her ear with her middle finger — tidy, insolent, free in front of everyone and only just now beginning to suspect she had been free for some time — and went to collect the man with the heavy, useless, perjuring purse, who was already, helplessly, beginning to smile.
